description: We sell software that screens CVs and ranks job applicants for interviews.

assessment.summary: CV screening and applicant ranking software falls under Annex III point 4(a) (recruitment or selection: analysing and filtering job applications, evaluating candidates). The system ranks applicants by evaluating personal aspects such as their work-related performance and abilities, so it profiles natural persons. This means the Article 6(3) exemption cannot apply and the system is always high-risk. Nothing in the description points to an Article 5 prohibited practice: for example, no emotion inference from candidates, which Article 5(1)(f) bans in the workplace. No Annex I product is involved. As the vendor selling it under its own name, the company is the provider and must meet the Article 16 obligations, including Section 2 compliance and Article 49(1) registration. Customers using it to hire are deployers and have their own Article 26 duties. No Article 50 duties are evident because the system does not chat with candidates or generate content. That would change if a candidate-facing chatbot were added.

steps.finding: Screening and ranking CVs is not one of the listed prohibited practices. The closest is Article 5(1)(f), emotion inference in the workplace, and the description gives no sign that the system infers candidates' emotions.

evidence.quote: (f) the placing on the market, the putting into service for this specific purpose, or the use of AI systems to infer emotions of a natural person in the areas of workplace and education institutions, except where the use of the AI system is intended to be put in place or into the market for medical or safety reasons;

steps.finding: The software is standalone HR software. It is not a safety component of, or itself, a product covered by Annex I harmonisation legislation.

evidence.quote: (a) the AI system is intended to be used as a safety component of a product, or the AI system is itself a product, covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I;

steps.finding: Screening CVs and ranking applicants for interviews is recruitment or selection of natural persons: it analyses and filters job applications and evaluates candidates (Annex III point 4(a)).

evidence.quote: (a) AI systems intended to be used for the recruitment or selection of natural persons, in particular to place targeted job advertisements, to analyse and filter job applications, and to evaluate candidates;
2. In addition to the high-risk AI systems referred to in paragraph 1, AI systems referred to in Annex III shall be considered to be high-risk.

steps.finding: Ranking applicants evaluates personal aspects of each candidate, such as their abilities and likely performance at work. That is profiling within the meaning of Article 3(52) and GDPR Art. 4(4). It also materially influences who is invited to interview. Under the last subparagraph of Article 6(3), the system is therefore always high-risk and cannot be exempted.

evidence.quote: Notwithstanding the first subparagraph, an AI system referred to in Annex III shall always be considered to be high-risk where the AI system performs profiling of natural persons.

steps.finding: As described, the system processes CVs for recruiters. It does not interact directly with candidates, generate synthetic content, or perform emotion recognition or biometric categorisation, so no Article 50 duty is triggered. A candidate-facing chatbot would trigger Article 50(1).

evidence.quote: 1. Providers shall ensure that AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons are designed and developed in such a way that the natural persons concerned are informed that they are interacting with an AI system, unless this is obvious from the point of view of a natural person who is reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect, taking into account the circumstances and the context of use.

steps.finding: The company sells the software, which means it places it on the market under its own name, so it is the provider. Its customers who use it to hire are deployers.

evidence.quote: (3) ‘provider’ means a natural or legal person, public authority, agency or other body that develops an AI system or a general-purpose AI model or that has an AI system or a general-purpose AI model developed and places it on the market or puts the AI system into service under its own name or trademark, whether for payment or free of charge;

obligations.text: Ensure the system complies with the Chapter III Section 2 requirements for high-risk AI systems: risk management, data governance, technical documentation, logging, transparency to deployers, human oversight, and accuracy/robustness.

evidence.quote: (a) ensure that their high-risk AI systems are compliant with the requirements set out in Section 2;

obligations.text: Design the system so that deployers can interpret its output and use it appropriately, and supply instructions for use.

evidence.quote: 1. High-risk AI systems shall be designed and developed in such a way as to ensure that their operation is sufficiently transparent to enable deployers to interpret a system’s output and use it appropriately.

description: A chatbot on our website answers customer questions about orders and returns.

assessment.summary: A website chatbot that answers customer questions about orders and returns is not a prohibited practice and falls in no Annex III area, so it is not high-risk. It interacts directly with natural persons, so Article 50(1) applies: people must be told they are talking to an AI system, unless that is obvious, at the latest at first interaction (Art. 50(5)). Tier: transparency. Role: the company uses the system under its authority on its own website, so it is a deployer. If it developed the chatbot itself (or had it developed) and put it into service under its own name, it is also the provider and the Article 50(1) design duty falls on it directly; otherwise it rests with the vendor. This does not change the tier. If the chatbot also produces synthetic content supplied by a GPAI provider, the Article 50(2) marking duty sits with the provider.

steps.finding: Answering customer questions about orders and returns uses no subliminal, manipulative or deceptive techniques, does not exploit vulnerabilities, and matches no other Article 5 practice.

evidence.quote: (a) the placing on the market, the putting into service or the use of an AI system that deploys subliminal techniques beyond a person’s consciousness or purposefully manipulative or deceptive techniques, with the objective, or the effect of materially distorting the behaviour of a person or a group of persons by appreciably impairing their ability to make an informed decision, thereby causing them to take a decision that they would not have otherwise taken in a manner that causes or is reasonably likely to cause that person, another person or group of persons significant harm;

(b) the placing on the market, the putting into service or the use of an AI system that exploits any of the vulnerabilities of a natural person or a specific group of persons due to their age, disability or a specific social or economic situation, with the objective, or the effect, of materially distorting the behaviour of that person or a person belonging to that group in a manner that causes or is reasonably likely to cause that person or another person significant harm;

steps.finding: Customer service for orders and returns is not in any Annex III area. It does not evaluate creditworthiness, set insurance pricing, decide eligibility for public benefits, act as a critical-infrastructure safety component, or serve law enforcement, employment, education, migration or justice.

evidence.quote: 2. In addition to the high-risk AI systems referred to in paragraph 1, AI systems referred to in Annex III shall be considered to be high-risk.

(b) AI systems intended to be used to evaluate the creditworthiness of natural persons or establish their credit score, with the exception of AI systems used for the purpose of detecting financial fraud;

steps.finding: The chatbot is intended to interact directly with customers (natural persons), so they must be told they are interacting with an AI system unless that is obvious, at the latest at first interaction.

evidence.quote: 1. Providers shall ensure that AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons are designed and developed in such a way that the natural persons concerned are informed that they are interacting with an AI system, unless this is obvious from the point of view of a natural person who is reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect, taking into account the circumstances and the context of use.

5. The information referred to in paragraphs 1 to 4 shall be provided to the natural persons concerned in a clear and distinguishable manner at the latest at the time of the first interaction or exposure. The information shall conform to the applicable accessibility requirements.

steps.finding: The company uses the chatbot under its authority on its own website, so it is a deployer. If it developed the chatbot itself and put it into service under its own name, it is also the provider. Article 25 is not triggered because the system is not high-risk.

description: An email spam filter that sorts incoming messages for our staff.

assessment.summary: An email spam filter that sorts incoming messages for staff is minimal-risk under the EU AI Act. It is not a prohibited practice. It is not part of an Annex I product. It falls outside every Annex III area: in particular, it does not recruit, evaluate, monitor or make decisions about workers. It has no Article 50 transparency duties, because it does not chat with people, generate content, or recognise emotions or biometric categories. The organisation uses it under its own authority, which makes it a deployer. The only general duty is Article 4 AI literacy. If the system were extended to monitor or evaluate staff behaviour or performance, it would need to be reassessed under Annex III point 4(b).

steps.finding: Filtering spam does not match any practice listed in Article 5, such as manipulation, social scoring, biometric scraping or emotion inference at work.

evidence.quote: 1. The following AI practices shall be prohibited:

(e) the placing on the market, the putting into service for this specific purpose, or the use of AI systems that create or expand facial recognition databases through the untargeted scraping of facial images from the internet or CCTV footage;

steps.finding: Sorting incoming email is not recruitment, a work-related decision, task allocation based on personal traits, or monitoring or evaluating workers' performance. It falls outside Annex III point 4 and the other listed areas.

evidence.quote: (b) AI systems intended to be used to make decisions affecting terms of work-related relationships, the promotion or termination of work-related contractual relationships, to allocate tasks based on individual behaviour or personal traits or characteristics or to monitor and evaluate the performance and behaviour of persons in such relationships.

steps.finding: The filter does not interact directly with people as a conversational system, does not generate synthetic content, and is not an emotion recognition or biometric categorisation system. No Article 50 duty applies.

evidence.quote: 1. Providers shall ensure that AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons are designed and developed in such a way that the natural persons concerned are informed that they are interacting with an AI system, unless this is obvious from the point of view of a natural person who is reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect, taking into account the circumstances and the context of use.

3. Deployers of an emotion recognition system or a biometric categorisation system shall inform the natural persons exposed thereto of the operation of the system, and shall process the personal data in accordance with Regulations (EU) 2016/679 and (EU) 2018/1725 and Directive (EU) 2016/680, as applicable.

steps.finding: The organisation uses the filter under its own authority for professional purposes, so it is a deployer. If it built the filter itself, it would also be the provider, but that does not change the tier.

evidence.quote: (4) ‘deployer’ means a natural or legal person, public authority, agency or other body using an AI system under its authority except where the AI system is used in the course of a personal non-professional activity;

obligations.text: Take measures to ensure a sufficient level of AI literacy among staff who operate or use the system (Article 4).

evidence.quote: Providers and deployers of AI systems shall take measures to ensure, to their best extent, a sufficient level of AI literacy of their staff and other persons dealing with the operation and use of AI systems on their behalf, taking into account their technical knowledge, experience, education and training and the context the AI systems are to be used in, and considering the persons or groups of persons on whom the AI systems are to be used.
